summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy, and esophageal varices was admitted for acute-on-chronic abdominal pain and distention. She also reported nausea, mild confusion, and absence of bowel movement despite lactulose use. Initial labs showed leukocytosis, and urinalysis revealed elevated white blood cells, prompting treatment for a presumed urinary tract infection with IV ceftriaxone, later switched to oral cefpodoxime. CT scan showed trace ascites and cirrhotic liver changes without acute intra-abdominal pathology. Furosemide was held initially due to low blood pressure but restarted. Her mental status improved with bowel regimen, and abdominal pain slightly improved. She was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics, continue liver and encephalopathy medications, and follow up with her primary care provider for colonoscopy and evaluation of beta-blocker use for varices.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
